doc.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Double bass drums and the great drummers
title: Twenty-inch bass drums and cymbal placement
summary: He explains choosing 20 x 20 bass drums over the 26-inch norm, keeping cymbals low like Jo Jones, and a story of Buddy Rich on Eddie Shaughnessy's kit.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Early drum kits and the gear drummers used

blocks.x: This picture of this Gretsch prototypical double-bass-drum set – you mentioned that you were using 20-inch bass drums . . .
20 x 20, which is a departure from what was pretty much the norm in those days.
What size were the bass drums being used at that time?
I was using the 26-inch bass drum. I’m using 24’s now.
But you went down to the 20. I guess that was to facilitate having two up there.

Yeah. I was thinking that the tubular – long tube would give me the sound I was looking for. Yet I could put those tom-toms on top of that 20-inch bass drum and not make everything too high, because I always wanted my cymbals to be in a position so I can play rhythm, because today some drummers have – I don’t know how they do that. They play with the cymbals very high, but they still get a sound. To me, I go with Jo Jones, who said, “I like that ride cymbal right there, staring me in the face.” And I like the Chinese cymbal right over here, and an 18-inch cymbal over here, so I’ve got three ride cymbals. I remember when Buddy Rich one time on the Tonight Show – Eddie Shaughnessy was playing drums. Eddie’s a big guy – he sat in on Eddie’s drums. He said he had to jump up in the air to hit one cymbal. Eddie got a big kick out of that.
